drills.q: Two assets, vols 20% and 5%, any correlation. Give ERC weights and the resulting capital tilt.
drills.a: w1 = 5/(20+5) = 0.2 on the 20%-vol asset, w2 = 0.8. Correlation cancels for N=2; each contributes exactly 50% of portfolio variance.

drills.q: Compute beta: Cov(stock, market) = 0.0009 daily, Var(market) = 0.0004 daily.
drills.a: beta = 0.0009/0.0004 = 2.25. High-beta name; CAPM would demand a large premium, but remember the flat-SML anomaly means realized compensation is usually lower than CAPM implies.

drills.q: Why does GMV not need expected returns while tangency does? Show both formulas.
drills.a: GMV w = Sigma^-1 1 /(1'Sigma^-1 1) uses only covariance; tangency w proportional to Sigma^-1(mu - rf) needs mu. Since mu estimates carry SE ~ sigma/sqrt(T), GMV is far more stable out-of-sample.

drills.q: A fund wants ERC at 10% vol using bonds (vol 5%) and stocks (16%). Estimate gross leverage.
drills.a: ERC two-asset mix vol ~6-7% unlevered (dominated by bond weight 76%); to hit 10% needs roughly 10/6.9 ~= 1.4x gross. In practice RP funds run futures/swaps leverage with margin lines sized for vol spikes.

drills.q: Your optimizer outputs +180% in one stock and shorts elsewhere. Diagnose and give three fixes.
drills.a: Classic error maximization / corner solution from near-singular Sigma plus noisy mu. Fixes: Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage; long-only with position caps and turnover penalty; Black-Litterman prior so views fight equilibrium only where you have real information.

drills.q: Explain in three sentences why a factor with backtest t = 2.4 deserves skepticism.
drills.a: With hundreds of tested characteristics, multiple testing alone yields many t > 2 by chance; Harvey-Liu-Zhu recommend t > 3 for novel claims. Published premia also decay post-publication due to crowding/arbitrage. Demand out-of-sample, cost-adjusted, capacity-aware evidence before allocating.

drills.q: 2022: SPX total return -18%, Agg -13%. Why did risk parity suffer more than the raw numbers suggest?
drills.a: RP levers the bond sleeve 2-3x to equalize risk, so the worst-ever bond year hit levered; simultaneously correlations flipped positive removing diversification; financing costs spiked as rates rose. Result: category drawdowns ~20-30% vs ~-16% for unlevered 60/40.

drills.q: Write the KKT system that traces the long-short efficient frontier exactly with numpy.
drills.a: Solve [[2Cov, mu, 1],[mu',0,0],[1',0,0]] [w,l1,l2]' = [0, r_target, 1]'. Sweep r_target over [min mu, max mu]; each solve gives one frontier point; filter negatives for the long-only approximation (clipping breaks exact optimality).

drills.q: PM says 'we hold 50/50 stocks and bonds, so our book is balanced.' One-sentence correction?
drills.a: Capital is balanced but risk is not: with 16%/5% vols, equities contribute ~90-95% of variance; balance requires equalizing risk contributions (ERC), which puts most capital in bonds.

drills.q: Design question: building a fully systematic robo-advisor portfolio module across 15 asset classes with no explicit human return forecasts, would you use mean-variance optimization, risk parity, or a hybrid? What would change your answer if a tactical view was later added?
drills.a: Prefer risk parity (or minimum-variance with constraints) as the systematic default -- with no return forecasts, mean-variance would either fabricate noisy historical-mean estimates (walking into the estimation-error-maximization problem) or degenerate into risk parity anyway. If a tactical view is later added (e.g. 'emerging markets will outperform'), Black-Litterman is the right upgrade: it layers the specific view onto a market-equilibrium-implied prior with explicit confidence weighting, avoiding both ignoring the view (risk parity can't use it) and naive mean-variance's instability from overweighting an unshrunk view.
